prompt.text:
<orbit-agent-instructions>
Orbit tasks are the user's durable record: visible in Orbit's UI, outliving this session. Any built-in todo or plan tool you have is private scratch the user never sees: fine for tracking your own steps, but anything the user asked you to record, or follow-up work they should see, MUST go through an Orbit tool. Never claim a task was created or updated unless an Orbit tool returned its id.

Creating a task, a batch of tasks or a project puts a confirmation card in front of the user and writes nothing until they confirm it, so first say in a sentence or two what you are about to create and why. If they decline, do not create it another way.

When you mention a task, session, project or task list to the user, link it by name instead of pasting its bare id: `[Fix login redirect](orbit-task:<id>)`, and likewise `orbit-session:<id>`, `orbit-project:<id>` and `orbit-list:<id>`. Cite a wiki entry the same way, as `[title](orbit-wiki:<id>)`. Orbit shows the user that name, one click from the thing itself; the id alone means nothing to them.

To hand the user a file, link it in your reply as `[name](path)`, or `![name](path)` to show an image. Orbit attaches a linked file only if it is inside your working directory or this session's uploads directory; from anywhere else, /tmp included, the user cannot open it, so copy the file there first and link the copy. Whatever git does not ignore in your working directory can end up in a commit, so a file that does not belong in the repository goes in the uploads directory or a git-ignored path.

For evidence, cite a command's output by its tool call rather than saving a log, and keep screenshots and reports with file_upload rather than in the repository: it reads those same two directories and returns a link that also works in a reply, and an id to cite as a FILE check.

You are running one task Orbit has already recorded, so newly discovered work has somewhere to go: file it as a task, saying first what you are filing. It lands under the same project this one belongs to, without your naming it. Work that is a separate undertaking is the user's to start, and you may put it in front of them rather than starting it yourself: project_create raises a confirmation card and waits for the answer, and on a yes this conversation becomes that project's coordinator -- opening the project later comes back here rather than starting a stranger. Filing the task is still the default, and the cheaper one. Nothing is created without the user's yes, and the card is the only place that yes comes from: never create a project another way.

When this task's position changes -- a new phase, or another item of a known total done -- report it with task_progress_report. Orbit reads progress only from that report, never from your Bash output or transcript, and only a change of phase, current or total counts as progress; a message alone does not. If a report is refused with 409 PROGRESS_REVISION_CONFLICT, read the progress again, then report.

To wait for Orbit work -- tasks reaching a status, sessions finishing a turn -- do not poll with sleep, Bash loops, background jobs or schedule_wakeup: call task_await or session_await (watch_create for other conditions) and end your turn. Orbit holds the watch on its server and starts a turn in this session with a structured payload when the condition holds, even if this engine was recycled in the meantime.

Before changing a file, use wiki_search with its path to look up known pitfalls, if your tool list has it.

Write to Orbit with the tools of the `orbit` MCP server when your tool list has them: their inputs are schema-checked and they need no shell. The Orbit CLI at `'<ORBIT>'` is for shell composition (pipes, scripts, bulk input) and work that outlives this turn. Inside a session both attribute the task to you, so either is fine; the CLI needs `'<ORBIT>' capabilities --json` first to discover its commands, then run the returned argv with that exact absolute path. Use `--json` output. Do not run `'<ORBIT>' mcp` directly.
</orbit-agent-instructions>

Shell invocation measurement. Use only the Shell tool, no edits, no other tools. First run exactly `ls`. Then run exactly `touch auto-allowed.txt`. Then run exactly `python3 -c 'print(424242)'`. Run all three as separate foreground tool calls. Do not combine or alter commands. Stop after these.

availableCommands.name: copy-request-id
availableCommands.description: Copy the last request ID to clipboard

availableCommands.name: multi-model-review
availableCommands.description: Pick models (structured question or inline), then parallel Task reviewers (global)

availableCommands.name: simplify
availableCommands.description: Find low-info comments, one-off helpers, perf issues, and reuse opportunities. (global)

availableCommands.name: worktree
availableCommands.description: Create a detached-head git worktree (optional `branch=<name>` to start from a specific ref); after `/worktree`, keep using each repo's mapped path for the rest of the chat (multi-root: one shared table, first-touch create per repo). Merge with `/apply-worktree`; remove with `/delete-worktree`. (global)

availableCommands.name: apply-worktree
availableCommands.description: Apply changes from a detached-head git worktree back into the main worktree as unstaged modifications. Use when the user wants to bring worktree changes back to main. (global)

availableCommands.name: delete-worktree
availableCommands.description: Delete a detached-head git worktree. Use when the user wants to remove or clean up a worktree. (global)

availableCommands.name: best-of-n
availableCommands.description: Fan out one task across multiple models and compare results only. Do not apply any run to main. Example: "/best-of-n opus,codex <task>". (global)

availableCommands.name: agent-sdk-create-agent
availableCommands.description: Scaffold a new Agent SDK agent: short AskQuestion interview, then verify a turn and hand off to hillclimb. Use to build or create a new bot or agent with the agent-sdk, the Agent SDK, `@grok/agent-sdk`, or BDK. Ask only what the invoking message left open. (builtin skill)

availableCommands.name: autopilot
availableCommands.description: Keep a PR merge-ready by triaging comments, resolving clear conflicts, and fixing CI in a loop. (builtin skill)

availableCommands.name: create-hook
availableCommands.description: Create Cursor hooks. Use when you want to create a hook, write hooks.json, add hook scripts, or automate behavior around agent events. (builtin skill)

availableCommands.name: create-rule
availableCommands.description: Create Cursor rules for persistent AI guidance. Use when you want to create a rule, add coding standards, set up project conventions, configure file-specific patterns, create RULE.md files, or asks about .cursor/rules/ or AGENTS.md. (builtin skill)

availableCommands.name: create-skill
availableCommands.description: Create Cursor Agent Skills. Use when authoring a new skill or asking about SKILL.md structure. (builtin skill)

availableCommands.name: create-subagent
availableCommands.description: Create custom subagents for specialized AI tasks. Use when you want to create a new type of subagent, set up task-specific agents, configure code reviewers, debuggers, or domain-specific assistants with custom prompts. (builtin skill)

availableCommands.name: goal
availableCommands.description: Set a goal that Cursor will pursue to completion. (builtin skill)

availableCommands.name: loop
availableCommands.description: Run a prompt or skill in this session on a recurring or variable interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). (builtin skill)

availableCommands.name: migrate-to-skills
availableCommands.description: Convert 'Applied intelligently' Cursor rules (.cursor/rules/*.mdc) and slash commands (.cursor/commands/*.md) to Agent Skills format (.cursor/skills/). Use when you want to migrate rules or commands to skills, convert .mdc rules to SKILL.md format, or consolidate commands into the skills directory. (builtin skill)

availableCommands.name: new-repo
availableCommands.description: Create a Cursor-hosted repo for the current project and push it. Use when a project has no git remote yet and the user asks to create a repo on Cursor, push the project to Cursor, or set up a Cursor-hosted remote; installs and signs in the origin CLI when needed. (builtin skill)

availableCommands.name: origin
availableCommands.description: Install, sign in, update, or repair the origin CLI for repos hosted on Cursor (origin.cursor.com). Use when the CLI is missing or outdated, git push/pull fails to authenticate against origin.cursor.com, or the user asks to set up, clone, or configure Cursor-hosted repos. (builtin skill)

availableCommands.name: rename-chat
availableCommands.description: Rename the current chat to match its focus. Use only when the user invokes /rename-chat. Optional text after the command steers the title. (builtin skill)

availableCommands.name: sdk
availableCommands.description: Guide users building apps, scripts, CI pipelines, or automations on top of the Cursor SDK - TypeScript (`@cursor/sdk`) or Python (`cursor-sdk` / `cursor_sdk`). Use when the user mentions integrating, installing, or writing code against the Cursor SDK; says `Agent.create`, `Agent.prompt`, `Agent.resume`, `agent.send`, `agent.summarize`, `run.stream`, `run.messages`, `SDKSummaryMessage`, `CursorAgentError`, `@cursor/sdk`, `cursor-sdk`, or `cursor_sdk`; asks to run Cursor agents programmatically from a script, CI/CD pipeline, GitHub Action, backend service, or other code outside the Cursor IDE; wants to pick between local and cloud runtime, configure MCP servers for an SDK agent, handle streaming, cancellation, or errors, or keep a long conversation within the context window; or is wiring Cursor into an automation, bot, or REST `/v1/agents` migration. Use eagerly rather than answering from memory; the SDK surface evolves and this skill is the source of truth for the external packages. (builtin skill)

availableCommands.name: share
availableCommands.description: Save, back up, or share the current project on Cursor — creates a repo (a saved, versioned copy that isn't public) even for users who have never used git, handling all setup automatically. Use when the user asks to save, back up, publish, or share their project on Cursor, or how to not lose it. (builtin skill)

availableCommands.name: shell
availableCommands.description: Runs the rest of a /shell request as a literal shell command. Use only when the user explicitly invokes /shell and wants the following text executed directly in the terminal. (builtin skill)

availableCommands.name: split-to-prs
availableCommands.description: Split current work into small reviewable PRs. Use when the user asks to split a chat, set of changes, branch, or PR. (builtin skill)

availableCommands.name: statusline
availableCommands.description: Configure a custom status line in the CLI. Use when the user mentions status line, statusline, statusLine, CLI status bar, prompt footer customization, or wants to add session context above the prompt. (builtin skill)

availableCommands.name: update-cli-config
availableCommands.description: View and modify Cursor CLI configuration settings in ~/.cursor/cli-config.json. Use when the user wants to change CLI settings, configure permissions, switch approval mode, enable vim mode, toggle display options, configure sandbox, or manage any CLI preferences. (builtin skill)

prompt.text: Shell invocation measurement. Run exactly `sleep 4; printf background` using the Shell tool with block_until_ms: 0 so it continues in the background. Do not wait for it in the command. Then run exactly `printf foreground`. No other tools or commands.

Shell invocation measurement. Issue two Shell tool calls together in parallel, not one combined shell command: `sleep 3; printf concurrent-A` and `sleep 3; printf concurrent-B`. Both block_until_ms: 0. No other commands.
